items.originalTitle: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
items.summary:
OpenAI's GPT-6 family of models can design protein shapes and amino acid sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using general reasoning and coding capabilities. In lab experiments with partner Onava, proteins designed by GPT-6.2 showed evidence of binding across five targets, and redesigned antibodies retained their binding ability. The models demonstrated the ability to incorporate instructions about protein attachment sites and shapes, suggesting they integrate knowledge from math, physics, chemistry, and biology to reason about protein interactions.

The research highlights GPT-6's versatility in protein design tasks, including predicting molecular interactions and ranking sequence changes, performing comparably or better than specialized models on most tasks except full protein structure prediction. The models can switch between tasks by changing prompts without retraining, enabling flexible guidance from atomic bonds to overall protein shape. This approach could simplify protein engineering by reducing the need for multiple specialized tools and expertise.

It updates models only when new versions outperform previous ones and ensures privacy by keeping all data on the user's machine without requiring accounts or telemetry.

Songe runs in the background, activating only when resources are free and pausing immediately when the user returns, aiming to provide seamless and private model improvement without disrupting normal workflows.

items.originalTitle: In Private Funding, Like IPOs, Big Companies Dominate
items.summary:
The private fundraising market in 2026 is increasingly dominated by the largest tech companies, whose combined valuations have more than doubled from $1.1 trillion to $2.6 trillion in a year, according to Goldman Sachs. This trend mirrors the IPO market, where only a few large offerings like Anthropic and SpaceX have gone public, but most are trading below their IPO prices amid a challenging environment for tech valuations.

Goldman Sachs highlighted companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Databricks, Stripe, and others as key players raising billions more, making it difficult for smaller startups to compete for investor attention. Despite public market declines, private valuations remain elevated due to strong revenue growth in AI businesses, even as many operate at a loss. Industry insiders remain cautiously optimistic about potential IPOs in 2027, including older venture-backed startups and AI-enhanced software firms.

items.originalSummary:
Shares of Anthropic fell below its $83 IPO price on Tuesday morning, summing up what has been a tough year for IPOs. While a couple of monster IPOs got done—Anthropic and SpaceX—only a handful of others made it through including offerings from SK Hynix, Cerebras and Lime. And as of Tuesday, all of those were trading below their IPO price. 

That makes it the fifth year in a row when the IPO market has been at least a bit disappointing. A bunch of companies are lined up for next year—including OpenAI—but slumping tech valuations fueled by skepticism about the AI boom clouds prospects for 2027. 

In that context, it’s a decent time to take the pulse of startup dealmaking. One thing is clear: as in the IPO market this year, in the private fundraising market, the biggest companies are sucking the oxygen out of the room.

The top 10 private companies have more than doubled their combined valuation from $1.1 trillion to $2.6 trillion in just one year, Goldman’s top tech banker Jane Dunlevie said on stage last week at Goldman Sachs’ annual private tech conference in Las Vegas. 

She was talking about OpenAI, Anthropic, Databricks, Stripe, Waymo, Revolut, Anduril, Ramp, Cognition and Jeff Bezos's Prometheus. And more than half of those—OpenAI, Databricks, Anduril, Stripe, Ramp and Cognition—are now trying to raise billions more.

That makes it tough for smaller startups. To be sure, Goldman did its best at last week’s conference in Las Vegas. The bank managed to play matchmaker for more than 400 investors and 400-plus startups in the gilded corridors at the Encore Wynn Hotel. 

Recent events raise another question: as public market valuations fall, how long until private valuations start to take a hit? 

One reason why private valuations can stay elevated even as public stocks drop is that venture investors tend to zoom in on growth. Many of these AI businesses’ revenues have taken off, even as they bleed money thanks to expensive AI models they run and the chips they need to buy or rent. 

At a fireside chat at last week’s confab, Winston Weinberg, CEO of legal AI startup Harvey, acknowledged that even with fast revenue growth, its gross margins fell to about negative 55% around June. They improved the figure by about 95% in roughly three months. Weinberg said annualized revenue grew from $190 million at the end of last year and expected to end this year with at least $675 million.

“We’re still early in the build out of AI, which means many of the defining companies of this era are not yet public and many investors are just getting to see the potential of those companies, both on growth and margin.” Goldman’s Jane Dunlevie said in an interview on the sidelines. 

She said each tech era has its own tests with investors: for internet companies, it was a path to profit; for subscription software firms, it was predictable revenue and net revenue retention. 

Meanwhile, attendees at the conference were staying hopeful about next year’s IPO market. Some predicted that older venture-backed startups, such as Vercel, Ramp and Plaid, and even the older vertical software companies with some AI makeover, such as AlphaSense and Clio, will finally go public.

In the two days of investors’ schmoozing over fancy desserts and cocktails, a lineup of popular AI, chip and cybersecurity startups, like Legora, Unconventional AI and Abnormal AI fielded dozens of investors’ meeting requests. Many older software startups were trying to remind investors they still exist. They are not getting too much love, say bankers and investors. 

One barometer of who’s important in Las Vegas this year was whom Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon invited to his private dinner at the fancy restaurant Delilah. In attendance: Legora CEO Max Junestrand and Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao, said people familiar with the dinner.

items.title: European Commission confirms AI-assisted cyberattack stole personal data from EU Academy platform, warns users via website notice [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: European Commission confirms personal data stolen in AI-assisted cyberattack
items.summary:
The European Commission confirmed that personal data, including names and email addresses, were stolen in an AI-assisted cyberattack targeting its EU Academy online learning platform. The breach was disclosed last week, and the Commission has posted a notice on the platform's website warning users of potential phishing and impersonation risks instead of contacting them directly. Access to the platform has been disabled until January 2027 as the Commission rebuilds it, requiring users to register anew without transferring previous coursework records.

The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor about the incident and is investigating the breach, which involved an AI-powered hacking tool linked to broader cyber espionage concerns. While some internal applications have been restored, others remain offline, and the Commission has not confirmed whether the attackers have been fully expelled. The approach to notifying affected users has drawn scrutiny, especially since the platform remains inaccessible during the notification period.

items.originalSummary:
I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.

Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.

Coding agents in November 2025

Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model.

In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:

Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.

This held up.

Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025.

Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant.

The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself.

Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.

The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work.

Fable class models in June/July

We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.

In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.

After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st.

For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these:

In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug.

A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm.

Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook.

I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well.

These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model.

3D modeling and game development in September/October

Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for.

I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example.

3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa.

Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game. It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play.

I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play!

Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked. My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay.

Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time.

Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games.

The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster.

It feels like another inflection point to me.

Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too?

I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement.

I'm getting so much done with that model right now!

It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42, 1.0a43, and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37, 0.37.1, 0.37.2, 0.37.3, and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks, represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements.

If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it. That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks.

Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand.

items.summary:
Locally hosted AI models offer advantages such as data privacy, no per-token API costs, and offline operation, but they suffer from lower reasoning capabilities, high hardware demands, slower inference speeds, and limited context windows compared to cloud-based models like GPT-5 or Claude. These limitations make local models less suitable for complex or large-scale applications despite their appeal for strict privacy, regulatory compliance, and predictable high-volume usage.

The article outlines key challenges including setup complexity, poor tool integration, and lack of real-time information in local models. It also discusses scenarios where local hosting is appropriate, such as for solo operators controlling costs or enterprises needing data residency compliance. However, the overall assessment is that local models are not a comprehensive solution and often cannot match the quality and scalability of cloud-hosted AI services.

items.originalSummary:
In its effort to win more business customers, OpenAI this fall launched an agent designed to help firms analyze their data and get answers to internal questions about their business. But at least one customer that has used the agent so far has found it isn’t yet accurate enough for widespread use.

That’s a big problem. But OpenAI isn’t sitting still. Representatives of the ChatGPT creator have told some customers and partners that they are developing a data management platform to help the agent perform better, according to the customer and three other people who spoke to OpenAI in recent weeks.

The data management platform, code-named Athena, has similarities to what is known in the industry as a semantic layer, which companies use to create standardized definitions for business metrics such as revenue and customers, one of the people said. This type of software helps agents understand the difference between gross revenue and net revenue, or active and paying customers, the person added.

One of the biggest reasons agents fail when companies use them with large amounts of complex business data is that they have to work out on their own what the data means and how it fits together, said Jason Strimpel, a managing director at Andersen Consulting who helps large companies use AI. 

“A semantic layer gives the agent that context from the start, often with plain-English descriptions of each item, so the agent has to guess less and [can work] faster and more accurately,” he said.

items.originalTitle: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
items.summary:
GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery

Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries:

With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library. It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians.

Here's the digitized sketchbook.

Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work.

Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue? Mark thinks it will be mild:

But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature.

Tech stocks, including Nvidia, were trading down early Tuesday, as the enthusiasm sparked by Jensen Huang’s unexpected reinstatement as CEO dissipated. Meanwhile, a series of high-profile cyberincidents in recent weeks have affected banks, government institutions and other critical infrastructure—including, most recently, the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s national crime database, which the White House confirmed over the weekend was targeted in a hack.

Though it’s still unclear whether AI played a role in some of these breaches, the attacks have intensified fears that the technology is emboldening cyber criminals. For OpenAI, this brewing fear around cybersecurity also represents something else: the company’s next big business opportunity.

The potential of cybersecurity as a revenue driver—as OpenAI seeks to bolster its finances ahead of a potential initial public offering next year—was a key theme that emerged from my conversations with OpenAI’s leaders for a profile of the company’s president, Greg Brockman, which we published last week.
